about: Reference recordings of wild barred owl (Strix varia), all from xeno-canto. Licenses were checked on each recording's own page on 2026-11-12. trimStartSec/trimEndSec are seconds in the original file as downloaded. Each clip keeps at least 0.3 s before the call for the noise floor (0.35 s, measured from the end of a quiet run). Calls were classified by measurement against the cited call definitions in callDefinitions; uncertain clips say so in notes. All recordings used say 'Playback used: no' on their page.

callDefinitions.readVia: shortcut: both sources were read through web-search excerpts, because this build environment's network blocks birdsoftheworld.org, bioone.org, academic.oup.com and the paper's open-access copies; quotes below are from those excerpts. Re-read the paper (its Figure 1 and Table 1) and the Birds of the World page directly before Phase 8 shows any of this text in the app.

odom-mennill-2010.title: Odom, K. J. & Mennill, D. J. (2010). A quantitative description of the vocalizations and vocal activity of the Barred Owl. The Condor 112(3): 549-560 (peer reviewed)
odom-mennill-2010.urlNote: DOI taken from the BioOne article URL; the DOI link itself was not opened.

bow-sounds.title: Birds of the World (Cornell Lab of Ornithology), Barred Owl, Sounds and Vocal Behavior

calls.name: Who cooks for you (two-phrase hoot)
calls.definition: Two sets of four syncopated notes, three short and one long; total duration 3.19 ± 0.07 s (Odom & Mennill 2010). The familiar 'Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?' (Birds of the World).
calls.use: Given often in spontaneous calling bouts and when an owl confronts other Barred Owls (Odom & Mennill 2010).
calls.classifyBy: 8 notes in two sets of four; the 4th note of each set is the longest; ~3 s.

calls.name: Ascending hoot
calls.definition: 6-9 regularly spaced, evenly accentuated, ascending syllables, followed by a downwardly inflected 'hoo-aw' (Birds of the World). Named as a separate call type, the ascending hoot, by Odom & Mennill (2010).
calls.use: Not stated in the excerpts read; no use is claimed here.
calls.classifyBy: evenly spaced short notes with no long note in the middle, rising in pitch, ending in a longer note that falls in pitch.
calls.caveat: A search summary also gave a typical length of ~8 s; that figure was not confirmed from a direct quote and is not used. The clips measured here are ~2.5-3.5 s from the first clear note.

calls.name: Hoo-wah (inspection call)
calls.definition: A single-syllable call that rises and then falls in pitch, 'hooooahh'; also known as the hoo-wah (Birds of the World). Named as the inspection call by Odom & Mennill (2010).
calls.use: Given by both sexes; considered a contact call; among the most frequent Barred Owl calls, given throughout the night (Birds of the World).
calls.classifyBy: one isolated note, ~0.5-0.8 s, pitch rises briefly then falls.
calls.caveat: Birds of the World notes the final 'hoo-aw' of the hoot series is very similar, so only isolated single notes were used.

calls.name: Caterwaul (duet)
calls.definition: Caterwaul bouts: a male and female calling in alternation (Odom & Mennill 2010, citing Mazur & James 2000). Monkey-like cackles, screams, wails and caterwauling duets (Birds of the World).
calls.use: Duets between the two owls of a pair (Odom & Mennill 2010).
calls.classifyBy: recordist label of caterwaul/duet, plus measured high notes (~1.0-1.4 kHz) mixed with low hoots (~0.4-0.6 kHz); hoots alone stay below ~0.75 kHz.
calls.caveat: Loose, variable category made by two birds; one person cannot make both parts. Likely hard to score; Phase 8 may keep it locked.

notIncluded: One-phrase hoot: named by Odom & Mennill (2010), but the excerpts read disagree on its note spacing, so no reliable definition to classify against.
Two-note and three-note hoots: named in the paper's results excerpt, no description found.
Wail / scream, alarm and juvenile begging calls: not requested for this phase.

clips.author: Scott Olmstead
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 (44.1 kHz mono) and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV. No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Measured: 8 notes in two sets of four: onsets 0.44, 0.79, 1.20, 1.37 s | 2.16, 2.48, 2.88, 3.07 s. In each set the 4th note is the longest (0.17 s in set 1, 0.38 s in set 2, others 0.09-0.15 s); gap between sets ~0.6 s. Call ~3.0 s (first onset to end of last note). Dominant frequency ~580-625 Hz throughout; last note falls in pitch at its end. Lead-in 0.35 s; SNR 34.3 dB (loudest frame vs 10th-percentile frame, 150-2000 Hz); peak sample 0.693 of full scale, no clipped samples. Recordist remarks: recorded through an open window during pre-sunrise twilight, 2026-05-31; animal not seen; no playback. Background: Veery, Hermit Thrush.

clips.author: John Middleton
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 (44.1 kHz stereo) and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV (stereo channels averaged). No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Measured: notes ~0.35 s apart (5 detected from 0.74 s), getting louder and longer (0.07 -> 0.15 s), dominant rising 581 -> 689 Hz, then a long (0.88 s) note that falls in pitch to ~470 Hz. Recordist calls it the 'Who cooks for you' song, but the measured structure is evenly spaced notes with no mid-call long note, which matches the ascending hoot, not the two-phrase hoot. Uncertain label: classified by measurement against the recordist's label. Lead-in 0.35 s; SNR 47.5 dB (loudest frame vs 10th-percentile frame, 150-2000 Hz); peak sample 0.733 of full scale, no clipped samples. Recordist remarks: 'Who cooks for you' song from a Water Oak at the edge of a cypress pond in early morning, 2020-04-02; animal seen; no playback. Background: Red-shouldered Hawk (not audible in this clip's time range by spectrogram).

clips.notes: Measured: one isolated note, 0.80 s (the only other sound event in the recording is the duplicate noted below). Contour: quick onset, pitch rises from ~590 Hz to ~635 Hz in the first 10-25% of the note, then falls to ~400 Hz by 75% (later frequency readings are echo/harmonic). A single rising-then-falling syllable, matching the inspection call ('hoo-wah'). Peak 0.39 of full scale. Lead-in 0.35 s; SNR 31.7 dB (loudest frame vs 10th-percentile frame, 150-2000 Hz); peak sample 0.392 of full scale, no clipped samples. Recordist remarks: two calls from a single individual perched about 5 m up, given after preening and stretching, 2021-10-29; animal seen; no playback. xeno-canto forum comment on this recording (wisconagus): 'Beautiful one note inspection calls.' The second call in the file (at ~32.4 s) is sample-identical to the first (cross-correlation 0.9999), so it was not used as a separate clip.

clips.author: Bruce Lagerquist
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 (44.1 kHz stereo) and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV (stereo channels averaged). No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Measured: two frequency layers: low hoot-like notes (~370-540 Hz) and a fast run of high notes at ~1.05 kHz, ~0.36 s apart (onsets 2.22, 2.59, 2.95, 3.30 s), with a 0.73 kHz note before them; the high layer is far above every hoot in this set (hoots stay below ~730 Hz). Recordist label: caterwauling of two birds. Uncertain: the measurement cannot show whether the high and low layers come from two birds, and caterwauling is a loose category; label rests on the recordist plus the frequency measurement. An earlier, louder part of this recording (17.5-21.9 s) was rejected: 129 samples at full scale (clipped in the original). Lead-in 0.35 s; SNR 30.4 dB (loudest frame vs 10th-percentile frame, 150-2000 Hz); peak sample 0.716 of full scale, no clipped samples. Recordist remarks: saw one bird fly to a roost near the second just as it was getting dark when the birds started caterwauling, 2018-04-25; animal seen; no playback.

Recordist remarks: caterwauling pair near a wetland and farm, 2020-09-24; sex female and male (recordist); animal not seen; no playback; recordist edits: trimmed and normalized to -3 dB; loud insects audible.
